claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast, multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct eutectic phases.
The eutectic phases have inherent electrochemical potential differences.
Mechanical sliding repeatedly ruptures protective oxide or passive films at eutectic phase boundaries.
Film rupture exposes fresh, compositionally dissimilar phase surfaces.
The exposed dissimilar phases form local galvanic couples.
Multiphase high-entropy-alloy structures can produce galvanic corrosion effects and inferior corrosion resistance.
Wear-induced exposure of galvanic phase couples accelerates localized corrosion.
Corrosion weakens the surface and makes it more susceptible to subsequent wear.
The reciprocal interaction between wear and corrosion establishes a positive feedback loop.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will cause greater total degradation than isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
Simultaneous exposure will increase wear depth relative to isolated wear.
Simultaneous exposure will increase corrosion rate relative to static corrosion.
The proposed mechanism requires mechanical stress sufficient to disrupt oxide films, a chloride-rich corrosive environment, and elevated temperature.
The synergistic acceleration may not occur at lower temperature, reduced load, or in non-aggressive media.
A simultaneous sliding-corrosion test can be compared with inert-environment wear and static-corrosion controls at matched temperature and, where applicable, matched mechanical parameters.
Failure of simultaneous exposure to produce degradation significantly greater than the additive isolated wear and corrosion effects would falsify the proposed synergy.
